articles.title: MLB World Series 2026 Storylines to Track in Rays vs. Brewers Fall Classic Bracket
articles.summary: The Tampa Bay Rays cashed their ticket to the 2026 World Series on Monday night with a 7-3 win over the Cleveland Guardians for the American League pennant, joining the National League champions, the Milwaukee Brewers.
articles.body:
The Tampa Bay Rays cashed their ticket to the 2026 World Series on Monday night with a 7-3 win over the Cleveland Guardians for the American League pennant, joining the National League champions, the Milwaukee Brewers.

Two fresh faces in the Fall Classic, neither team is the star-studded squad baseball fans have come to expect after two straight seasons of the Los Angeles Dodgers hoisting the Commissioner's Trophy, but that is not necessarily a bad thing.

Ahead of the greatest series in sports, find out the stories to track and more in this preview.

When the Rays and Brewers take to the field in Game 1 of the World Series on Friday night at 8:00 p.m., they will do so having never won the most coveted prize in baseball.

Both have been to the dance, Tampa as recently as 2020, but neither has gotten over the proverbial hump and won the title.

Either Milwaukee will capture its first championship since its founding in 1969, or the third time will be the charm for the Rays.

Tampa played the Dodgers and Phillies in the Fall Classic, but has never mustered the level of performance that got them there. They lost decisively to Philadelphia in 2008, 4-1, and did not fare much better against the Dodgers 12 seasons later (4-2).

The Brewers' lone World Series appearance came in 1982, when they lost in seven games to the St. Louis Cardinals.

It was difficult to find a starting pitcher who had a worse first half of the season than Freddy Peralta.

The New York Mets traded for the ace in the offseason, only to watch him develop a 4.99 ERA and become a liability on the mound.

With the season cratering, they sent the righty to the Rays, where he quickly reversed fortunes, going 5-2 in 10 appearances, with an ERA of 3.25 and a WHIP of 1.01, both vast improvements from what fans in Queens had seen from him.

His redemption continued into the playoffs and, ultimately, the ALCS, where he was named the MVP after going 2-0 with a 0.75 ERA and recording 9 strikeouts.

Up next for the 30-year-old? A date with his former squad, Milwaukee, for whom he played eight seasons and earned two All-Star appearances.

After a disastrous start, what better way to wrap things up than by beating the team he spent the majority of his career with and winning the Rays their first World Series ring?

The Brewers' Longtime Leader Gets His Title Shot

Christian Yelich joined the Milwaukee Brewers following a 2017 trade and quickly became the face of the franchise. He won the NL MVP award in 2019 and earned "captain" status with the organization as its leader, both in front of the cameras and behind the scenes.

He has been through the highs and the lows with the team, and while he may not be quite the player he once was, there is no denying that he is as synonymous with this generation of the Milwaukee squad as anyone.

After a season that saw him deliver 104 hits, 12 home runs, 59 RBI, and a slash line of .235/.315/.378, it will bear watching as to whether or not Yelich still has that superstar magic left in him and can help propel his organization to its first world championship.

A close friend of the late Brewers play-by-play announcer, the legendary Bob Uecker, Yelich figures to be playing for teammates both here and gone when he takes to the diamond Friday night at American Family Field.

articles.title: MLB Fan's Jumbotron Message Rejecting Relationship Shown in Viral Photo From Rays-Guardians
articles.summary: Getting friend-zoned is one thing, getting friend-zoned in public is another, but getting friend-zoned during an ALCS closeout game in front of over 40,000 fans could be the most understandable villain origin story of all time.
articles.body:
Getting friend-zoned is one thing, getting friend-zoned in public is another, but getting friend-zoned during an ALCS closeout game in front of over 40,000 fans could be the most understandable villain origin story of all time.

While most fans at Tropicana Field celebrated the Tampa Bay Rays advancing to the World Series with a 7-3 win over the Cleveland Guardians, a poor soul named Derek was left with a jumbotron message thanking him for tickets to Monday night's game but rejecting his offer for a relationship:

Surely this message could've been delivered privately, but Derek will now live on in infamy after the rejection photo went viral.

Hopefully, the Rays can provide some solace to Derek as they seek their first World Series title against the Milwaukee Brewers.

articles.title: Rays star Freddy Peralta achieves historic pitching feat only accomplished twice since 1913
articles.summary: Tampa Bay Rays star Freddy Peralta joined Hall of Famers Bob Gibson and Walter Johnson with a feat seen just twice since 1913 as the ALCS MVP eyes a World Series.
articles.body: When you do something on the baseball field that’s only been done twice in nearly 114 years by two Hall of Famers, you know it’s extraordinary. Tampa Bay Rays star and ALCS MVP Freddy Peralta has been lights out down the stretch. In his last 10 starts dating back to the regular season, he has pitched more than 50 innings, allowed one run or fewer in each start, and his team has won all 10 games, according to Opta STATS. The only two other pitchers to have such streaks were St. Louis Cardinals legend Bob Gibson in 1968 and Walter Johnson in 1913 with the Washington Nationals. However, Johnson’s Nationals are not today’s Nationals. The franchise later became known as the Washington Senators before moving to Minnesota and becoming the Twins in 1961. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE When the Rays acquired Peralta from the New York Mets at the trade deadline, he had a 4.99 ERA in 22 starts. While they expected him to improve, no one could have expected this. "This is crazy," Peralta said. "I’m very happy to be here and grateful to be here because when I was in July, I had no idea where I was going to be. I think that this was the right place." Since joining the Rays, the 30-year-old went 5-2 in 10 regular-season starts with a 3.25 ERA and was named the American League’s Pitcher of the Month for September. In the postseason, he has been especially dominant. In four appearances (three starts), Peralta has a sparkling 1.08 ERA in 16 2/3 innings pitched. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Nicknamed "Fastball Freddy" for his heater, Peralta credited Rays pitching coach Kyle Snyder, along with bullpen coach Jorge Moncada and bullpen catcher Charlie Valerio, for his turnaround. "They helped me a lot," Peralta said. "I can’t thank them enough because the way that they helped me is amazing, something I’m never going to forget in life. I’m very grateful to have people like that here, people that I never saw before and now they are part of my family." While Peralta is on a roll, the World Series is going to be a little odd for him: He will face the Milwaukee Brewers, with whom he spent the first eight seasons of his career. "But this is a time to compete ... and excited to go." The right-hander is set to hit free agency this offseason and could earn a big payday. First, however, he is looking to take down his old team and help the Rays win their first World Series title. The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: MLB player will become World Series champion regardless of Brewers-Rays outcome
articles.summary: Jake Woodford played for both the Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays this season, guaranteeing he becomes a 2026 World Series champion.
articles.body: The World Series hasn’t started yet, but one player is already a champion. Relief pitcher Jake Woodford played for both the Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays this season, guaranteeing that he becomes a champion. The Rays traded the 29-year-old to Milwaukee just before the season began in March. Woodford was in the Brewers’ bullpen to start the season, appearing in 16 games. He had a 1-0 record with a 6.94 ERA and one save in 23 1/3 innings pitched. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE On June 5, Woodford was designated for assignment and subsequently released a few days later. On July 4, he signed a contract with the Chicago Cubs. Woodford appeared in just one game for the Cubs, allowing three runs in two innings. The Cubs designated Woodford for assignment on July 11, and he was released on July 16. However, the Cubs signed him to a minor league contract on July 18. On July 29, the Cubs selected his contract, returning him to the major league roster. Woodford threw one scoreless inning on Aug. 3 but was once again designated for assignment by the Cubs on Aug. 4 and released on Aug. 10. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! The Rays then brought him back, signing him to a minor league contract on Aug. 11. After more than a month in the minor leagues, the Rays selected his contract and added him to their major league roster on Sept. 24. Woodford pitched against the New York Yankees, giving up three earned runs in 1 1/3 innings. He was designated for assignment on Sept. 25 and released again on Sept. 29. Woodford’s roller-coaster ride took him through three different teams over the course of the 2026 season, but one of those teams is guaranteed to win the World Series. There is no official rule that requires teams to give rings to every player, as ring distribution is at the discretion of team ownership and management. The World Series begins on Friday at 8 p.m. ET, with the Brewers hosting the Rays.

articles.title: Rays vs. Brewers World Series preview: Who has the edge in matchup of MLB's 2 best teams?
articles.summary: It's Jacob Misiorowski and the Brewers against Junior Caminero and the Rays beginning Friday in the Fall Classic.
articles.body:
Since the MLB postseason began on Sept. 29, 12 teams have played 35 games to get to this point. Just two teams remain in the field.

It's the top-seeded, 98-win Tampa Bay Rays against the top-seeded, 103-win Milwaukee Brewers in the World Series. Neither team has ever won a title. Game 1 begins at 8 p.m. ET Friday in Milwaukee.

Here's everything you need to know about the matchup.

Rays: The owner of the best record in the American League this season, Tampa Bay goes about it with a fascinating combination of stars, contact-heavy role players and magnificent defense. Their offensive top three of Junior Caminero, Yandy Díaz and Jonathan Aranda has been a force to be reckoned with all season, with the bottom of the lineup stepping up just enough so far this postseason. The Rays cleanly dispatched the Yankees in an ALDS sweep before charging back from down 2-1 to win three straight ALCS games against a pesky Guardians team .

Brewers: The Brewers have arrived in the 2026 World Series as the most dominant team this postseason. They finished the regular season with an MLB-best 103 wins and have continued to show that was no fluke, losing just one game so far this October. Milwaukee took down the San Diego Padres in a series that showcased their resilience against a star-studded lineup and their tenacity against one of baseball's best bullpens.

But it was their NLCS rematch against the back-to-back World Series champion Los Angeles Dodgers that showed everyone that these aren't the same ol' Brewers. Milwaukee dominated the Dodgers across four games, not only beating them but sweeping them . After becoming the first team in MLB history to sweep a team that swept them the previous postseason, the Brewers are not messing around as they seek the franchise's first World Series title.

Catcher: Liam Hicks (TB) vs. William Contreras (MIL)

It's Contreras, but it's closer than you think. Hicks has been one of the most impactful bats moved at the trade deadline, posting a .774 OPS for the Rays down the stretch and into October. He has been particularly potent against righties (.840 OPS) and, most importantly, has done a great job behind the dish handling the Rays' pitching staff. Hicks' third-inning ABS challenge in ALCS Game 6 was an under-the-radar game-changer in Tampa Bay's pennant-clinching win.

Still, Contreras gets the edge because, well, he has been the best hitter in this postseason. Among players who reached the LCS, Contreras' 1.157 OPS ranks first. His defensive work can be a bit volatile at times, but the offensive impact is downright undeniable. Scared of the big moment? No, the big moment is scared of him.

First base: Jonathan Aranda (TB) vs. Jake Bauers (MIL)

Aranda, the least famous member of Tampa's big three alongside Yandy Díaz and Junior Caminero, has generally stepped up during the Rays' October run. Eight singles, a homer, a walk and three HBPs are nothing to sneeze at.

But there's no way to pick against Bauers, the NLCS MVP and this postseason's breakout star. His deep-count battles against Dodgers pitching were instrumental in Milwaukee's crisp dispatching of the two-time defending champs. And Bauers' hot postseason is simply a continuation of his phenomenal regular season. He was the best hitter on baseball's best team this year; no reason to make it more complicated than that.

Second base: Richie Palacios/Ben Williamson (TB) vs. Brice Turang (MIL)

Ask a Milwaukee front-office character who the club's best player is right now, and chances are they'll say Turang. The 26-year-old is a wonderful sum-of-the-parts character, a sensational defender with a well-rounded offensive game. His freakish opposite-field homer off Tarik Skubal in NLCS Game 1 got the party started for the Brewers, but don't forget about the defensive gem he unleashed on the very first play of that game. Turang isn't your prototypical danger man, but he's a magnificent player capable of impacting things in a number of ways.

Palacios, who came up huge in ALCS Game 6 , starts against righties, while Williamson, more of a glove-first type, hops in for southpaws.

Shortstop: Taylor Walls (TB) vs. Cooper Pratt (MIL)

Still just 22 years old, Pratt, the soda-chugging rookie, has impressed this October with a barrage of singles and a howitzer right arm. The ease with which he uncorks throws from deep in the hole could one day earn him a Gold Glove.

Walls, however, is already the best defensive shortstop in the sport. Defensive metrics disagree somewhat on his value, but ask any team official for a peek at their internal data, and Walls will almost certainly be at the top of the leaderboard. He has a preternatural feel for batted-ball direction, spin and velocity as it relates to a given pitch, meaning he's often in the correct position or moving in the correct direction before contact. Offensively, Walls is just pesky enough to be useful. Typically, nothing good happens when he swings, but he can draw a walk, lay down a bunt and move a runner over. That's just a bonus because his glove is a legitimate game-changer.

Third base: Junior Caminero (TB) vs. David Hamilton/Joey Ortiz (MIL)

Caminero and Hamilton, who starts against righty arms, are currently tied with one playoff home run apiece. Things were a bit more unbalanced during the regular season: Caminero cranked 38 more taters than the light-hitting Hamilton.

Game 6 homer aside , Caminero hasn't exactly taken the world by storm this October. He entered the clincher 7-for-30 with just two RBI, three extra-base knocks and no big flies. That's a terrifying proposition for the Brewers — the idea that Caminero is still waiting to erupt. But don't get it twisted: This is his team, his moment, his stage. He wants to be the guy and is certainly wired right and talented enough to deliver another magical moment or three.

Left field: Chandler Simpson/Ryan Vilade (TB) vs. Jackson Chourio (MIL)

Simpson's slash-and-dash approach is the only one of its kind in baseball right now, making him perhaps the most entertaining at-bat in this entire World Series. Any ball hit on the ground is a potential single. Any single is a potential stolen base. And if Simpson is standing on second, he's a guaranteed run on anything to the outfield. Vilade is the opposite style of player; he's on the roster to mash left-handed pitching, and that's really it.

But Chourio, still just 22, wins any showdown, even though he's coming off a sneaky subpar NLCS. He's hitting a cool .171/.211/.343 in October, but most of his knocks have been extremely timely. Chourio's backside bomb off Blake Snell on the first pitch of NLCS Game 3 was as big of a crowd silencer as we've seen in a while. This guy has teetered on the precipice of stardom for a while; this series could push him over the edge and into the larger American sporting consciousness.

Center field: Jonny DeLuca (TB) vs. Garrett Mitchell (MIL)

Two of the game's more impressive athletes, DeLuca and Mitchell can absolutely run it down in center. But while DeLuca hit 11 homers in the regular season, his offensive game is a lot more dink and dunk, while Mitchell, as he showed in the NLCS , has real thump in his bat. A barrage of injuries over the past few seasons prevented Mitchell from breaking through into regular playing time. Now finally healthy, he's making the best of his mountain of talent.

Right field: Victor Mesa Jr. (TB) vs. Sal Frelick/Luis Lara (MIL)

This one is a toss-up. Offensively, none of these three has been particularly integral thus far in October. Mesa had a huge homer in NLDS Game 3 against New York, and Frelick's three singles and four walks have helped keep the line moving for Milwaukee, but generally, these are secondary lineup pieces. Out in the grass, however, Mesa, Frelick and Lara have all been key characters. Mesa's right arm is a weapon; anytime he gears up to uncork one, runners stop dead in their tracks. Lara and Frelick, meanwhile, are center fielders playing right field.

Designated hitter: Yandy Díaz (TB) vs. Christian Yelich/Andrew Vaughn (MIL)

Díaz's eighth-inning bomb in ALCS Game 6 provided perhaps the most celebratory and cathartic moment in Rays franchise history. But even though he is built like a bodybuilder, his game is built more on smoking the ball to all parts of the field than on lofting it over walls. Still, he's dang good at that schtick; nobody in these playoffs has collected more base hits than Tampa Bay's muscled-up DH.

Brewers skipper Pat Murphy's decision to sit Yelich twice against left-handed starters in the NLCS speaks volumes about what type of hitter Milwaukee's captain is at this point in his career. That's not a knock on Yelich; he has remained relatively productive against righties despite a laundry list of injuries and has delivered a few big knocks so far in October. Murphy's move also says a lot about Vaughn, a former top pick who has revitalized his career in Milwaukee. He obliterates lefties, but with Tampa Bay's righty-heavy staff, Vaughn probably won't get a start in this World Series. Will the game find him for a big showdown in the later innings?

Rotation: Drew Rasmussen/Freddy Peralta/Nick Martinez/Griffin Jax (TB) vs. Jacob Misiorowski/Logan Henderson/Robert Gasser/bullpen extravaganza (MIL)

Milwaukee has the NL Cy Young favorite, but Tampa Bay has the superior starting staff. In fact, Misiorowski, for all this triple-digit majesty, underwhelmed in both of his postseason starts . He kept scoring to a minimum but failed to finish five innings against both San Diego and Tampa Bay. Not exactly ace behavior. Rasmussen, meanwhile, worked eight, six and seven innings in his three postseason outings, surrendering three total runs across those 21 frames. The two probably won't face off in Game 1, with Rasmussen having pitched Sunday in ALCS Game 3, making World Series Game 2 the likelier option for him.

If that's the case, the Rays will send Nick Martinez to the mound opposite Misiorowski, which would make for a wonderful stylistic juxtaposition. The veteran righty has emerged as perhaps the most crucial character in Tampa Bay's clubhouse, but he's also enjoying a career year in his age-35 season. He covered 180 regular-season innings with a 3.10 ERA and made the All-Star team thanks to elite control and a sinker-heavy, high-groundball approach. ALCS MVP Freddy Peralta should get the rock in Game 3. After a disastrous first few months with the Mets following a trade from Milwaukee last winter, Peralta latched on with Tampa Bay at the deadline. At the time, the Rays got some love for adding Peralta, but nobody expected him to rediscover himself to this extent. He has allowed two runs over 16 ⅔ innings this postseason.

After Misiorowski, Milwaukee's rotation turns to Henderson, whom the Brewers refused to part with at the deadline in talks regarding Tarik Skubal. The 24-year-old Texan pitched well in his Game 2 start against Los Angeles, but two throwing errors on balls to first derailed his evening and left four runs (two earned) on his ledger. A few more deep breaths, and Henderson might have pitched deep into that evening. Gasser looked outstanding in Game 3 at Dodger Stadium, almost certainly earning him a World Series start. Game 4 will be a bullpen affair for the Brewers featuring a combo of Dustin May, Shane Drohan and Chad Patrick.

Bullpen: Bryan Baker/Kevin Kelly/Cam Booser/Tyler Wells (TB) vs. Trevor Megill/Abner Uribe/Aaron Ashby/DL Hall (MIL)

Brewers take the edge here. Their bullpen has allowed just six earned runs over 40 ⅔ innings of postseason work, with 38 strikeouts to boot. Trim that group down to the top four of Megill, Uribe, Ashby and Hall, and the numbers are even more impressive: 0.61 ERA in 29 ⅔ frames. Tampa Bay closer Bryan Baker has been absolutely dynamite in the ninth, but the road to him has been shaky at times. Booser, Wells and Kelly have shown well, but Ian Seymour coming undone in the ALCS clincher portends poorly for Tampa. Their secret weapon? Rookie Brody Hopkins has just six MLB outings under his belt but has some of the nastiest stuff on the planet. He has yet to feature, but could provide one of the more electric moments of this Fall Classic.

The matchup of managers is an intriguing one between the Rays' Kevin Cash and the Brewers' Pat Murphy. If there's an edge between the two, it comes from their experience. Cash is not only baseball's longest tenured manager but also has managed the Rays in the World Series before (in 2020). Known for his quick thinking and in-game strategy, even if it's sometimes to the chagrin of the public, he's never going to be surprised.

On the other side, Murphy has quickly become one of the best managers in baseball, having won manager of the year in his two prior seasons at the helm and likely to be a finalist again this year. So far in October, Murphy has outmanaged Padres skipper Craig Stammen and Dodgers manager Dave Roberts. He'll find the matchup he's looking for and has shown he's not afraid to pivot if something isn't working. Murphy will have another tough challenge ahead of him strategizing against Cash.

Rays: The Rays' starting rotation should keep them in ballgames; that much feels bankable. But for Tampa to top the hard-charging Brew Crew, they'll need their big three to carry the day. Díaz needs to stay hot, and Aranda and Caminero have to turn the dial up further. Milwaukee's deep, talented pitching staff should be capable of shutting down the bottom of Tampa's lineup. The burden, then, falls on the top trio to grab the spotlight and make magic happen.

Brewers: So far in this postseason, the Brewers have executed well on their recipe for success. Offensively, it's using their speed and ability to grind at-bats to wear teams down and tack on runs. On the mound, it's getting the ball to their electric bullpen and shortening games. Both have been extremely successful in October. Milwaukee has been hot offensively, and in this World Series, they'll need their offense, led by William Contreras and Jake Bauers, to continue to produce, as the Rays' starting staff is arguably the best they've seen this postseason.

But if the Brewers hope to win their first World Series, they'll need the best out of superstar fireballer Jacob Misiorowski. It's hard to believe the Brewers are four wins away from winning the World Series and "The Miz" hasn't completed five innings in a start this postseason. That will have to change if his team is going to hoist the trophy.

Rays: If the Brewers continue playing like they have so far this postseason, this will be an uphill battle for the Rays. Tampa Bay is a talented, well-built club with an underrated starting staff, three stellar hitters and a phenomenal defensive unit. But Milwaukee has them beat in terms of raw baseballing talent. If the Brewers' relentless offensive approach breaks through the bridge to Bryan Baker, Tampa could be in for a few late-inning messes and a decidedly short series.

Brewers: If things go wrong for the Brewers in this World Series, it will be because their starting pitching and bullpen falter. Neither Misiorowski nor rookie right-hander Logan Henderson has pitched well this postseason, and that lack of innings has forced Milwaukee to go to the bullpen a lot. While the relief crew has been successful thus far, as we've seen with the Padres, Guardians and Dodgers, even the strongest bullpens wear down due to overuse. If Milwaukee can't get at least 15 outs from Misiorowski and Henderson in each of their starts, by the end of the World Series, the Brewers' mighty bullpen will be a shell of itself. And while the Brewers' offense has been the best of any team this postseason, running into the red-hot duo of Drew Rasmussen and Freddy Peralta could be the thing that slows Milwaukee down.

Brewers in 5: The Brewers were trailing, at one point or another, against a two-time defending champion in all four of their NLCS victories. By that, they appeared entirely unperturbed. That relentlessness, that undauntedness, that short memory, that sheer sense of self-belief, gives Milwaukee the definitive edge. Their roster also happens to be better. — Mintz

Brewers in 6: Rarely in baseball do we get a World Series between two organizations that mirror each other, but when you look at the Brewers and Rays, it's hard to ignore the similarities. Speed, athleticism, elite pitching and a surprising amount of power are hallmarks of both teams. Still, one team seems to have a little extra motivation.

The Brewers are rolling, and nearly every area of their roster is clicking. The only one that hasn't been is their starting pitching, and to this point, that hasn't mattered. After back-to-back mediocre outings from the likely NL Cy Young, the law of averages would say a dominant performance is on the horizon.

The Rays are a worthy opponent for Milwaukee, and when the two best teams in the sport meet, we should expect a back-and-forth affair. But this Milwaukee team has shown it will not be denied, and it's hard to see that changing in this World Series. — Dorsey

articles.title: $131 Million All-Star Pitcher Atlanta Braves Should Consider Trading For
articles.summary: Should the Atlanta Braves consider trading for Toronto Blue Jays‘ starter Jose Berrios? Berrios has been a very durable starter in the past, but a Tommy John...
articles.body:
Should the Atlanta Braves consider trading for Toronto Blue Jays' starter Jose Berrios?

Berrios has been a very durable starter in the past, but a Tommy John Surgery in 2026 puts his future in jeopardy.

However, with that being said, it could be something for the Braves' front office to consider, as the Blue Jays may want to get off what's left of his seven-year, $131 million contract (about $48 million), and the asking price on Berrios could be at an all-time low.

Berrios has been the subject of trade rumors in the past, and for a starting pitcher-hungry team, Atlanta stands out as a potential fit.

Jose Berrios isn't necessarily a trade candidate, but he could emerge as one very quickly if the Blue Jays announce to other teams that they would be willing to take on some of his contract to offload him.

If so, the Braves, who are expected to be active in MLB's external market this offseason, could be a team to take a flyer on the 2X MLB All-Star.

The Blue Jays just don't necessarily need his services anymore, and likely aren't counting on him to be part of their rotation plans in 2027.

However, you never know in MLB what pitchers will go down with injury, underperform, etc., so it's always a luxury to have a plethora of capable arms.

Also, there is familiarity between the Blue Jays and Braves, as Alex Anthopoulos served as Toronto's GM before joining the Braves.

articles.title: Bengals vs. Ravens bold predictions for AFC North clash in Week 7
articles.summary: For the Cincinnati Bengals, Ja’Marr Chase saved some money by appealing. As for the Baltimore Ravens, their kicker is on notice. These teams meet in a Week...
articles.body:
For the Cincinnati Bengals , Ja'Marr Chase saved some money by appealing. As for the Baltimore Ravens , their kicker is on notice. These teams meet in a Week 7 AFC North clash, and here are bold predictions for the contest.

The Bengals (3-2) enter the game in last place in the division despite having a winning record. That's because the Ravens, Steelers, and surprising Browns all have a record of 4-2.

It should be another battle for the Ravens and Bengals.

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

Joe Burrow will riddle the Ravens' defense for 3 TD passes

When the Bengals are right, they are tough on offense. And they've been cooking this year, ranking No. 9 in the NFL in points per game.

Burrow is connecting on 71.4% of his passes. He has 11 touchdown passes and three interceptions. Look for him to keep the momentum going this week. But Burrow needs to take care of the football, which Zac Taylor said would go a long way in helping the Bengals win, according to Cleveland.com.

"The turnovers is what screams at you," Taylor said. "That leads into field position."

And Taylor said Burrow and his teammates are ready for this matchup.

"It's exciting," Taylor said. "I think our guys really get fired up for this game. Not that they don't get fired up for every game, but whenever we play in Baltimore in a road divisional game, it's a fun one to get up for, and our guys will be up for it."

Bengals RB Chase Brown will score two TDs

One of them will be on the receiving end of a pass from Burrow. Brown will have a nice day, despite being caught in a time share with Samaje Perine, according to The Athletic.

"I think we'll continually assess how that touch share between (Perine) and Chase Brown should play out," Bengals offensive coordinator Pitcher told Geoff Hobson of Bengals.com. "Every game's different. What type of scheme we lean into is going to factor into that. Obviously, what we ran more of yesterday leans into what Samaje does well, which is get downhill and run through contact."

The Bengals haven't forgotten about their ground game.

"You strive for balance when it comes to run-pass," Pitcher said. "You're always wanting to be the most balanced and versatile version of yourselves. It's like those are high-level goals that you set out to attain. But never in any given situation are we going to let a high-level theoretical goal get in the way of what it means on Sunday to win a game and what is the feedback we're getting in a game on a given Sunday."

Derrick Henry will rush for 80-plus yards and a TD

Henry is still smarting from last week's fumble that led to the Ravens' loss to the Browns. He took blame for the game-changing turnover , according to ESPN.

"I got to take care of the ball," he said. "There's no excuses for that. I got to be better. I put the team in harm's way. I sound like a broken record with this, but I got to go back to work on it. Can't put the team in that situation."

Teammate Kyle Hamilton took up for Henry.

"Obviously, he's Derrick Henry, Hall of Fame running back [who] wants to hold onto the ball," Hamilton said. "He knows that. He's his harshest critic, so I'm not going to say anything ill about it. He's put us in position to win a lot of games."

All of this will motivate Henry for a big game against the Bengals

Ravens WR Ja'Kobi Lane will catch 5 passes and score a TD

Lane looked ready to roll against the Browns in his return from injury. And he should be able to carve out a significant role in Week 7. Lane looked great in training camp. The injury short-circuited his 2026 season. But now he's back in the mix.

His overall stat line could be impacted if Tyler Huntley is still at quarterback. But if Jackson is back, this could be a breakout game for Lane.

The Bengals should be able to outscore the Ravens in this matchup. But the key factor is Jackson. If he's back, the Ravens have a much better chance of winning.

But we will still roll with Burrow, Chase, and Tee Higgins having a big game, along with Brown doing his thing.

articles.title: Have MLB home run celebrations gone too far? Junior Caminero's long run around the bases sparks debate
articles.summary: Junior Caminero's 39-second home run trot in ALCS Game 6 reignited Major League Baseball's fierce debate over unwritten rules and showboating.
articles.body: Major League Baseball is viewed as one of the more traditional sports, along with golf, where an expected standard developed over 150 years of history. But things change over time, and in recent years, there's been a concerted effort to allow players to show more personality, be more demonstrative, and celebrate their success. Some pitchers now demonstrably react after striking out opposing hitters, to varying degrees. Mets reliever Jefry Yan being the most prominent example. Many hitters are now more willing to wear their emotions on their sleeve, in moments big and small. How you feel about this can relate to your age, the generation you grew up watching, or willingness to change with the times. But there are celebrations, and then there are celebrations. Monday night, in Game 6 of the American League Championship Series between the Tampa Bay Rays and Cleveland Guardians, we had the latter. RAYS PUNCH THEIR TICKET TO THE WORLD SERIES, TAKING DOWN GUARDIANS IN GAME 6 TO SET UP SERIES WITH BREWERS Needing a win to get to the World Series, the Rays were up 3-1 in the bottom of the seventh inning, facing Cleveland's best reliever, Cade Smith. Caminero came up with a runner at first and nobody out, crushing a line drive to left that hit the foul pole for a two-run homer. A huge moment for the 23-year-old second-year player that put his team one step closer to a championship. And Caminero enjoyed it. Really, really enjoyed it. At nearly 39 seconds, it was the second-slowest home run trot in the Statcast tracking era, per MLB.com's Sarah Lang. 39 seconds! To run the bases. And it's not just Caminero. In game two of the NLCS between the Los Angeles Dodgers and Milwaukee Brewers, catcher William Contreras hit a game-tying home run in the bottom of the fifth and, again, admired it and took an extraordinary amount of time to get around the bases. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE Reactions to Caminero's example were, well, mixed, to say the least. ESPN's Jeff Passan posted the video on X, "This is how you celebrate a home run in a game that could send you to the World Series. Junior Caminero is ready." Other fans called it a "disgrace," comparing it to how Derek Jeter would celebrate a big homer. One fan wrote, "Junior Caminero is a disgrace to the game of baseball. Imagine someone on the Yankees acting like this in a big playoff game. Imagine playing in the same division as Derek Jeter and acting this classless. There’s an argument that the Rays should bench Caminero. This isn’t how you act." Another had a similar sentiment, calling it a "slap in the face" to baseball. STAY "FEARLESS" ON THE GO! TAKE TOMI LAHREN WITH YOU. DOWNLOAD THE TLIF PODCAST NOW! "An absolute disgrace to baseball and everything this great game stands for! I first saw this video when Fry Daddy posted it, and I still can’t believe what I witnessed. Congratulations to both teams—one has a chance to win its first World Series, and that’s awesome. But what he did was an embarrassment, a complete disgrace, and a slap in the face to the game I love." No other sport has the number of "unwritten" rules that baseball has traditionally had in place. Don't show up the other team being one of them. But the celebrations this postseason raise the question, should those "rules" exist in the first place? OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD There are two valid sides to it; one says that baseball is about tradition and big celebrations are against the tradition of celebrating like you've been there before. The other is that players showing their personalities and emotions is important to modernize the game and bring in fans who enjoy seeing how much the moment means. Even Shohei Ohtani, who is rarely demonstrative, had a big celebration after hitting a home run in game four of the NLCS. Cade Smith, the closer who gave up the homer to Caminero, was asked his thoughts about the celebration after the game and had a magnanimous answer, saying, "It's not my style but I guess if I don’t like it, I shouldn’t give up home runs." Videos of Caminero's home-run, uh, walking trot, exploded on social media, and isn't that what MLB wants? Fans who don't normally see baseball to get the passion and energy and excitement that the postseason brings? On the other hand, though, is that the best example of it? Though, again, if you're going to celebrate anything, a huge home run to give your team a stronger chance to reach the World Series is probably the time to do it. Caminero and Contreras will have a chance to celebrate in the actual World Series when it starts on Friday. Just imagine if one of them hits a walk-off homer.

articles.title: Brewers' president of business operations sides with Timeless Ticket holders: 'We did not live up to the spirit of the program'
articles.summary: The 2015 program allowed 1,000 fans to purchase a $1,000 ticket redeemable for the best available seat at any one future Brewers home game of their choosing.
articles.body:
The Milwaukee Brewers unveiled a 2015 program called "Timeless Ticket." The program was simple: 1,000 people could pay $1,000 each for the chance to sit in the best available seats at any future home game, including the postseason

Eleven years later, the program proved anything but simple. It recently got the franchise in some hot water with disgruntled program members. Fans went to cash in their ticket and were reportedly offered seats in the fourth level, or standing-room-only seats, which they hardly considered "best available."

Milwaukee Brewers president of business operations Rick Schlesinger addressed this controversy and actually sided with the fans.

"We subsequently erred in our internal communications on the logistics of fulfilling the requests. While we were able to accommodate all with seats, we received feedback from some that they were unhappy with their seat locations. Clearly, even with extraordinary limitations on available seats, we did not live up to the spirit of the program and we have been working through a resolution. We regret our mistake and look forward to welcoming them to American Family Field for their World Series experience."

"We subsequently erred in our internal communications on the logistics of fulfilling the requests. While we were able to accommodate all with seats, we received feedback from some that they were unhappy with their seat locations. Clearly, even with extraordinary limitations on available seats, we did not live up to the spirit of the program and we have been working through a resolution.

We regret our mistake and look forward to welcoming them to American Family Field for their World Series experience."

Brothers Kevin and Kyle Deaton were among these fans hoping to cash in for the World Series, but were not OK with the seat selection they were offered.

"When you promise somebody the best seat available, and you give them pretty much the worst seats that you have in the whole stadium, I would say, no. They're not honoring it. I wasn't envisioning, hey, we're going to get front row. But certainly first ten rows. Which is why I refused. Out of principle, I'm not even going to go. This has to be a mistake. It's terrace level; that's level four. That's not the best available seat. And she said, yeah, I'm not going to argue that there's better seats available. This is what's being allocated to the 'Timeless Ticket' holders."

I wasn't envisioning, hey, we're going to get front row. But certainly first ten rows. Which is why I refused. Out of principle, I'm not even going to go.

This has to be a mistake. It's terrace level; that's level four. That's not the best available seat. And she said, yeah, I'm not going to argue that there's better seats available. This is what's being allocated to the 'Timeless Ticket' holders."

Milwaukee said fans who got these subpar seats could still attend the World Series, keep their Timeless Ticket, and redeem it for a game in any future season.

Milwaukee won 103 regular-season games, the most by any team in MLB. The Brewers clinched the No. 1 seed in the postseason, earning a bye through the wild-card round.

The Brew Crew then faced the San Diego Padres in the National League Division Series and won 3-1. This set up a big matchup with the two-time defending World Series champion Los Angeles Dodgers.

Milwaukee swept LA 4-0 in the best-of-seven series and now has a chance to win the franchise's first World Series championship if it can beat the Tampa Bay Rays.

articles.title: World Series is Full Circle for Brewers' Bauers, Rays' Peralta
articles.summary: Tampa Bay Rays' Freddy Peralta and Milwaukee Brewers' Jake Bauers face their original franchises in the 2026 World Series.
articles.body:
Back in 2018, a young man named Freddy Peralta made his MLB debut with the Milwaukee Brewers .

Peralta was 22 years old at the time, and he would enjoy a lengthy eight-year stint with the Brewers.

Knowing the team wouldn't be able to pay him what he wanted, Milwaukee traded Peralta going into the 2026 season, but things did not go great for him with the New York Mets .

Peralta was traded during the middle of the season, and he ended up on a Tampa Bay Rays team that just won the American League Championship Series.

Not only that, but Peralta was named the ALCS MVP as he got the win in the series-clinching Game 6 and made three overall appearances.

Talk about full circle: Jake Bauers, the NLCS MVP , made his MLB debut in 2018 for none other than the Tampa Bay Rays.

That was the only year Bauers would play for Tampa Bay, but it's still crazy to think that these are the two Championship Series MVP's, and now they're set to do battle against the team they made their MLB debuts for.

Peralta's lone start against the Brewers in his career came when he was with the Mets on Monday, July 20.

It was his second-to-last start with the Mets, and he fell to 5-9 on the year in a 5.1-inning outing that saw him throw 107 pitches.

Peralta allowed seven earned runs on eight hits, and it's clear the Mets left him in the fire as they needed depth and had little to no trust in their bullpen.

His return to American Family Field saw him strike out six batters. Cooper Pratt's first career big-league homer came off the former Brewers ace, and Andrew Vaughn went yard in this one as well.

Bauers was selected No. 208 overall back in 2013 by the San Diego Padres , the team Milwaukee beat in a four-game NLDS.

He was traded to the Rays ahead of the 2015 season and would eventually make his major- league debut on June 7, 2018.

On December 13, 2018, the Rays traded him to the then Cleveland Indians, another full-circle moment as the Rays just took down the Cleveland Guardians in a stellar six-game ALCS.

The Brewers are the fifth team Bauers has played for in his big-league career, but he's in the midst of his best season ever, and it's not even close.

articles.title: Jeff Passan believes MLB will play in 2027, but there’s a catch
articles.summary: MLB is in a difficult position. Momentum has been trending in the right direction over the past few years as interest in the sport seems to be growing. Howev...
articles.body:
MLB is in a difficult position. Momentum has been trending in the right direction over the past few years as interest in the sport seems to be growing. However, the potential of a lockout is looming as MLB and the MLBPA do not seem to be close to agreeing to a solution to the league's salary cap desire . A lockout would unquestionably be a detriment to baseball's momentum. The good news is that Jeff Passan of ESPN believes baseball will be played in 2027 — it just remains to be seen when the season will start given the seemingly inevitable lockout.

"Yes," Passan responded when asked if baseball will be played in 2027, via John Fanta of NBC Sports. "We will see baseball in 2027. When will we see baseball? That's a question that I don't have the answer to… I'm not trying to, like, avoid the question. I think a lot of it depends on what happens December 2nd and beyond, after the lockout, which I think is an inevitability at this point."

There was a fairly similar situation in 2022 when MLB and the MLBPA were working toward a new collective bargaining agreement. While there were differences in opinion then, this year's new CBA discussions seem to have a greater chance of leading to a longer lockout given how different both sides seem to feel about a salary cap.

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

There's more to both sides' argument, but to summarize, MLB has argued that a salary cap would level the playing field while the MLBPA is concerned that a salary cap would limit how much money players can make. Players want to ensure they are being paid fairly while the league wants to give every team an equal chance to sign the best players in free agency.

The momentum for baseball is real, so the shorter the lockout the better. Or, if they can somehow avoid a lockout (which seems highly unlikely), that would be ideal.
